SUBJECT:  Short-Term Rental Legislative Measures

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Adopt an ordinance repealing and replacing Article 3 of Chapter
1 of Title 3 of the Avalon Municipal Code modifying the Transient Rental System.

BACKGROUND: This ordinance was introduced and all further readings were waived on August
5, 2025.

On July 30, 2025, the approximate 24-month moratorium on the issuance of transient rental
licenses will end. City Staff have proposed an amendment to the Article 3 of Chapter 1 of Title 3
of the Avalon Municipal Code (AMC) Modifying the Transient Rental System. If adopted
regulations will go into effect 30 days later.

During the moratorium period, City Staff worked to cull through more than 40 years of short-term
rental historical documents in order to create a singular, short-term rental database.

City Staff has completed efforts to identify and revoke any existing, inactive or otherwise non-
compliant short-term rental properties granted by either grandfathered status, Conditional Use
Permit (CUP), or Transient Rental License (TRL).

Though initially 94 properties were brought before the Planning Commission for revocation, 31
properties challenged the revocation process, and two properties were found to have been
previously revoked.

Fourteen properties from the initial revocation list were able to come into compliance either by
providing proof of long-term lessee in the unit, or otherwise curing.

To date, either voluntarily or by Planning Commission action, a total of 77 short-term rentals
have been revoked, including:
  -  20 grandfathered units
  -  54CUPs
  -  3TRLs

On July 15, 2025, the City Council had detailed discussions of options for transient rentals. Two
agenda reports were then presented and such reports are attached hereto and incorporated into
this report.
 As of the July 15, City Council meeting, the City had identified a total of 386 compliant short-
term rental properties, including:

  •  91 properties permitted by grandfathered use (including 9 banked units currently occupied
  by year-round renters),
  •  267 properties permitted by CUP (including 13 banked units currently occupied by year-
  round renters), and
  •  28 properties permitted by Transient Business License (including 1 banked units currently
  occupied by year-round renters).

Therefore, there are currenUy 363 active short term rentals and 23 inactive (banked) properties.
Of the 363 compliant properties, 32 reported the minimum activity (2 nights) leaving 331 active
short-term rentals.

City Staff are continuing to analyze and monitor short-term rental properties. As properties are
found in non-compliance, they will be brought before the Planning Commission for revocation.

COMMUNITY FEEDBACK STAFF ACTIONS AND CITY COUNCIL DIRECTION AND ACTION

Amendments to the ordinance were based on feedback gathered from community meetings, an
analysis of other municipal ordinances, a community sentiment survey, and concurrence with
the Planning Commission. Specifically, the City focused on addressing quality of life issues for
residents, financial benefits and impacts to the local economy, and other sustainability and
affordable housing impacts associated with transient rentals.

Community feedback cited a need for a better regulatory process for short-term rental properties.
Utilizing the new database of rentals, in May, the City expanded its short-term rental monitoring
contract with Host Compliance to establish a 24/7 call center to support and provide oversight
of short-term rental complaints. The support line will provide a live notification system for property
managers as well as track property manager responsiveness, and the number and nature of
complaints filed for each property. City Staff is currently working with Host Compliance in the
development of the call center. It is anticipated the 24/7 call center will be activated by Fall 2025.

In addition to better enforcement and regulation, members of the community have recommended
establishing a cap to the number of short-term rentals in Avalon as well as a limit to the number
of short-term rentals owned by an individual or entity.

Each new transient rental license potentially takes a residential unit that could be used for long
term residency off the housing market. Given the shortage of available housing units in Avalon,
especially affordable units, limitations on the issuance of new licenses will preserve housing
stock available to residents.

At the City Council meeting on July 15, 2025, the City Council directed that such a cap be
established at 410 transient rental units. This includes all grand-fathered transient rental units,
all units with conditional use permits and all units with transient rental licenses.
 At the July 15 meeting there was also discussion on limiting the issuance of transient rental
licenses based upon whether the applicant has other transient rentals. The use of housing units
as transient rentals is an ancillary use to a residential use, not a commercial use. The ordinance
has been clarified to limit the issuance of transient rental licenses to applicants whose use of
such rentals will be ancillary to residential uses and not commercial uses. Thus, if the Planning
Commission determines that the use of a transient rental license will be commercial, it may deny
the license. While not a blanket ban on an applicant having more than one transient rental unit,
if the applicant has another unit or units, the Planning Commission should determine if such
requested license is for commercial purposes and can deny a permit if the use is primarily
corn m ercia I.

Because of the limit on new transient rental license permits, the ordinance provides that
procedures be developed for the issuance of such licenses when available permits become
available once the cap is reached.

The City Council also discussed and directed staff to include substantial penalties for violations
of the Municipal Code’s provisions pertaining to transient rentals and violations of conditions at
approval.

A state statute exists that provides for criminal penalties for violations of transient rental
regulations. Pursuant to Government Code §39000(a) certain violations related to threats to the
public health and safety, can be punishable by fines of $1 500 for the first violation $3,000 for
the second and $5,000 for each additional violations of it occurs within a year of the first violation.
Violations that do not constitute a threat to the public health and safety are punishable by fines
of $100 for the first violation, $200 for the second violations and $500 for each additional
violations that occurs within one year of the first violation. The proposed ordinance incorporates
these provisions.

At the August 5 meeting, the City Council modified the language of the proposed ordinance to
provide that if there are three adjudicated violations of the transient rental provisions or
conditions of use within a year, the transient permit or license must be revoked. The ordinance
allows the body revoking the permit to establish is owner can reapply for a transient license
rental in the future and set a time for such consideration.

The revised ordinance also incorporates the City Councils’ requirement that applicants for new
license must attend the Planning Commission meetings before such license is considered.

City will also work with the Planning Commission on the consideration of placing an overlay on
certain areas of the City where saturation of transient rental units may exists.

City Staff are currently performing an analysis of administrative costs associated with the
regulation of the City’s short-term rentals, permits and licenses. Once completed Staff will

  § 3-1.30. Purpose.
  The purpose of these transient license regulations is to establish a comprehensive regulatory
  framework for transient licenses within the City of Avalon for properties rented for fewer than 30
  days. The City recognizes that short-term rentals contribute significantly to economic
  development and allow visitors to experience the unique island community of Avalon and assist
  in providing access to the coast.
  Because residential transient rentals are an accessory residential use, and to safeguard the public
  health and safety and mitigate potential negative impacts to nearby residents, the regulations
  herein balance the benefits of transient rentals and impacts they may have upon adjacent
  residential uses. These regulations also limit the number of transient rentals to ensure the
  availability of full—time residential housing stock in the City, a critical concern given the inherent
  limitation on new construction and available property for residential development.

  Collection systems containing lift stations all have the

  • The buildup of FOG (fats, oils and grease)

  below, the FOG and debris. This allows the waste to collect
  closer to pump intakes and cause premature damage to the
  pumps. Short cycling and premature pump failure is also
  common under these conditions.
